title: Design with lines, circles, and triangles
learning_goals: Construct geometric figures from stated constraints using compass, straightedge, ruler, or dynamic geometry.
Use properties of perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, circles, and triangles to justify construction steps.
Test a conjecture by measuring or dragging a dynamic construction without treating measurement alone as proof.
success_criteria: I distinguish required constraints from decorative choices before constructing.
I explain why each construction step creates the intended geometric property.
I verify the result with independent measurements or properties and identify whether my evidence is a proof, check, or conjecture.

vocabulary.meaning: a condition such as a fixed length, angle, tangency, parallelism, or point location that a construction must satisfy
a line that crosses a segment at its midpoint and forms right angles with the segment
a ray or line that divides an angle into two angles of equal measure
the set of all points that satisfy a stated geometric condition
software that preserves construction relationships while points are moved to test which properties remain invariant

why_it_matters: Construction turns geometry from a picture into a set of relationships. Architects, machinists, drafters, surveyors, designers, and digital-model builders need to distinguish a shape that merely looks right from one whose constraints are actually encoded and can be checked.

direct_instruction.heading: Translate the design into constraints
direct_instruction.body: List every requirement before drawing: for example, two endpoints must be equally distant from a centre line, an arc must pass through two points, or a triangle must have a specified side and angle. Separate these requirements from choices such as page orientation or colour so the construction can be judged by geometry rather than appearance.

direct_instruction.heading: Construct from invariant relationships
direct_instruction.body: Use compass arcs to create equal distances, intersections to locate points satisfying two conditions, and straight lines through verified points. A perpendicular bisector works because every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints. An angle bisector can be built from equal-radius arcs because the paired construction transfers equal distances into equal angles.

direct_instruction.heading: Verify without confusing check and proof
direct_instruction.body: Measure lengths and angles, inspect symmetry, or drag points in a dynamic construction to look for failures. These checks can expose errors and support a conjecture. A justification goes further by connecting the construction steps to known geometric relationships. Record both the practical check and the property that explains why the result should hold.

method_routes.title: Constraint-first compass-and-straightedge route
steps: Rewrite the problem as a list of geometric constraints and known points or lengths.
Choose a construction operation that encodes each constraint, such as equal-radius arcs or a perpendicular bisector.
Mark every new point from an explicit intersection or defined distance rather than visual estimation.
Connect the constructed points and label the relationships created.
Verify dimensions and explain which geometric property guarantees each required condition.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route when the design must remain valid from stated lengths, angles, equal distances, or intersections without relying on a coordinate grid.
method_routes.check: Every required feature must trace to a construction step and geometric property, not merely to a ruler measurement after drawing.

method_routes.title: Dynamic-geometry conjecture-and-test route
steps: Build the figure using exact relationship tools rather than freehand placement.
Measure the target lengths or angles and state a conjecture about what remains constant.
Drag allowed points through several configurations while preserving the construction constraints.
Record any counterexample or stable pattern and identify which dependencies explain it.
Translate the dynamic evidence into a property-based justification or revise the conjecture.
method_routes.when_useful: Use this route when changing a figure can reveal which relationships are invariant and which were artifacts of one drawing.
method_routes.check: A property is not accepted merely because several dragged examples agree; explain the construction dependency or present the result as a tested conjecture.

representations.label: Labelled construction diagram
representations.description: A sequence diagram shows compass arcs, intersection points, line segments, equal-distance marks, right-angle marks, and the final constrained figure.
representations.text_alternative: Read each construction step in order, naming the starting points, radius or relationship used, intersection created, final connection, and verified property.

representations.label: Property-and-justification table
representations.description: Rows pair each required constraint with the construction operation, observable check, and geometric property that explains why the constraint holds.
representations.text_alternative: For every design requirement state the construction step, measured check, property justification, and any remaining tolerance or drawing limitation.

worked_examples.prompt: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment AB without measuring its midpoint first.

steps.label: Create equal-distance intersections
steps.explanation: Set a compass radius greater than 3 cm and draw arcs centred at A and B so the arcs intersect above and below the segment.

steps.label: Join the intersections
steps.explanation: Draw a straight line through the two arc intersections; both points are equally distant from A and B.

steps.label: Justify the result
steps.explanation: The locus of points equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector, so the new line crosses AB at its midpoint and at 90 degrees.

worked_examples.answer: The line through the two equal-radius arc intersections is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
worked_examples.verification: Equal compass radii encode equidistance from A and B; the locus property provides the justification independent of how the diagram looks.

worked_examples.prompt: A dynamic triangle has two sides constrained equal. Investigate whether the base angles remain equal as the vertex moves.

steps.label: Encode equality
steps.explanation: Construct the movable vertex as an intersection of equal-radius circles centred on the two base endpoints so the two side lengths remain equal.

steps.label: Test configurations
steps.explanation: Measure the base angles and drag the vertex through several valid positions; the two measured base angles remain equal within display precision.

steps.label: Explain the invariant
steps.explanation: The triangle remains isosceles because the side equality is a construction dependency, and the isosceles-triangle theorem explains the equal base angles.

worked_examples.answer: The dynamic evidence supports the invariant that the base angles are equal whenever the two constrained side lengths are equal.
worked_examples.verification: Dragging tests for accidental geometry, while the isosceles property explains why the angle equality holds for every valid configuration.

misconceptions.claim: A construction is correct if the final picture looks symmetric.
misconceptions.correction: Visual appearance is only a check; the construction must encode the required relationships and justify them.

misconceptions.claim: Measuring 90.0 degrees once proves two constructed lines are always perpendicular.
misconceptions.correction: A single measurement checks one drawing; the construction relationship or theorem explains the invariant.

misconceptions.claim: A compass is only for drawing decorative circles.
misconceptions.correction: Compass arcs encode equal distances and locate points satisfying distance constraints, making them a core construction tool.

guided.prompt: Which construction locates all points equidistant from endpoints A and B?
guided.rationale: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equally distant from the segment endpoints.

guided.prompt: A 70° angle is bisected. What is the measure of each new angle?
guided.rationale: An angle bisector divides the original angle into two equal parts.

guided.prompt: Explain why equal-radius arcs from A and B can help construct the perpendicular bisector of AB.

criteria: states arc-intersection points are equally distant from A and B
connects equidistance to the perpendicular-bisector locus
response.sample_response: Each arc intersection is the same compass radius from A and from B. Points with equal distance to the two endpoints lie on the perpendicular bisector, so two such intersections determine that line. Measuring the midpoint or right angle can then check the drawing.

guided.rationale: The explanation links the compass operation to the locus property that guarantees the result.

options: the circle must pass through point P
place it near the page centre
response.correct_answer: the circle must pass through point P

independent.rationale: Passing through a specified point is a geometric condition that can be tested.

independent.prompt: What is the safest conclusion after a dynamic construction keeps one angle equal through many drags?

options: it supports a conjecture that still needs property-based justification
the theorem is proven by the screen
response.correct_answer: it supports a conjecture that still needs property-based justification

independent.rationale: Repeated dynamic checks are strong exploratory evidence but do not replace a general justification.

independent.prompt: A circle has centre O and radius 4 cm. How far is every point on the circle from O?
independent.rationale: A circle is the locus of points at a fixed radius from its centre.

independent.prompt: Which step best verifies a constructed angle bisector?

options: measure both resulting angles and explain the equal-distance construction
rotate the paper until it seems even
response.correct_answer: measure both resulting angles and explain the equal-distance construction

independent.rationale: A numerical check plus the construction property gives both practical and logical evidence.

independent.prompt: Describe a construction plan for a triangle with base AB = 8 cm and the third vertex 5 cm from both A and B.

criteria: uses a circle or arc radius 5 cm from each endpoint
uses an intersection as the third vertex
notes two possible mirror solutions when valid
response.sample_response: Draw AB = 8 cm. With compass radius 5 cm, draw arcs centred at A and B. Either intersection can be the third vertex C, producing mirror-image solutions. Join C to A and B and verify that both new sides are 5 cm; the compass construction already encodes those equal distances.

independent.rationale: Two distance constraints are solved by the intersection of two loci, making the construction reproducible.

retrieval.prompt: What line divides a segment into two equal parts at a right angle?
retrieval.rationale: A perpendicular bisector combines midpoint and right-angle properties.

retrieval.prompt: What does a compass copy reliably in a geometric construction?
retrieval.rationale: A fixed compass opening transfers the same radius or distance to another location.

retrieval.prompt: Why is a property-and-justification table useful after a construction?

criteria: connects each requirement to a construction step
explains why the condition holds beyond appearance
response.sample_response: The table forces each design requirement to point to the step that created it, a measurement or visual check, and the geometric property that guarantees it. That makes it easier to find a missing constraint or a figure that only looks correct.

retrieval.rationale: The table separates encoded geometry, checking, and justification so the construction is auditable.

reflection_prompt: Which part of your construction is guaranteed by a geometric relationship, and which part did you only check by measurement or dynamic dragging?

accessibility.nonvisual_route: Every construction diagram is paired with ordered steps that state starting points, compass radii, intersections, line connections, equalities, right angles, and the property used to justify the final figure.
response_options: spoken construction algorithm with property table
